justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around recent price action. For the 1-day horizon, I set the estimate close to the prevailing market level, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over very short windows and that no major scheduled catalysts were imminent. The slight upward drift in the 1-week estimate reflects the general tendency for equity markets to carry a small positive drift premium over short horizons, consistent with historical daily returns averaging slightly above zero. By the 1-month horizon, I allowed the estimate to drift a bit further upward while acknowledging that a longer window gives more room for both secular trend and mean-reversion forces to interact, so the point estimate essentially extrapolates a modest continuation of whatever trend was in place at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to realized volatility. For a broad equity index or ETF in the 460–470 price range, daily moves of roughly 1–2% are common, which explains the relatively tight 35-point band at the 1-day horizon. As the horizon extends to a week and then a month, uncertainty compounds in roughly a square-root-of-time fashion, which is why the 1-month interval is nearly three times as wide as the 1-day interval. I also factored in that equity volatility tends to be somewhat fat-tailed relative to a Gaussian assumption, so I widened the intervals slightly beyond a pure volatility-scaling exercise to account for jump risk and regime shifts.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include unexpected macroeconomic data surprises — a sharply worse-than-expected jobs report or CPI print could trigger a move well beyond the lower bound, while a dovish policy pivot or strong earnings surprise could push prices above the upper bound. Geopolitical events, sudden liquidity dislocations, or a credit event in a systemically important institution represent tail risks that are by definition hard to price in advance. At the 1-month horizon in particular, a shift in Federal Reserve communication or an unexpected escalation in trade or military conflict could easily produce a move exceeding 15%, which would breach the stated interval entirely.

It is also worth noting that my intervals implicitly assume a relatively stable volatility regime. If realized volatility spikes — as it does during market stress episodes — the actual distribution of outcomes widens considerably. Conversely, if markets enter a low-volatility grind, the realized range could be much narrower than my intervals suggest. In short, these estimates are best understood as a reasonable central scenario with symmetric fat tails, not a precise prediction of where prices will land.
